sample.universe: Collective organizations active in the videogame industry and individuals working in it, in four metropolitan areas of three countries: Copenhagen (Denmark), Milan (Italy), Utrecht and Amsterdam (the Netherlands)
sample.unit_of_observation: interview (with a collective organization, or with an individual employee, freelance worker or employer); country case for the comparison
selection_rules: Denmark, Italy and the Netherlands selected because all are characterized by relatively strong IR actors and practices, while differing remarkably in their IR institutions (Scandinavian, Mediterranean and Continental models)

first phase: 30 interviews with collective organizations active in the industry - trade union representatives at local and national level, representatives of associations of freelance workers, officials of business organizations (employer organizations and trade associations), representatives of professional organizations, organizers of web-based networks

second phase: 43 interviews with individuals in the sector (employees, freelance workers and employers, often combining several positions), selected for the broadest possible representation of types of businesses and employment: sectors of activity, types of companies, contractual forms and activities
interview data supplemented with publicly available documents: legislation, policy statements, campaign material, newsletters, social media and web pages
sample.n_observations: 73 interviews (30 with collective organizations, 43 with individuals)
sample.n_individuals: 43 individuals interviewed (employees, freelance workers and employers)

construction_notes: NO Danish administrative register data are used. The article names no register and no register variable: the empirical material is 73 semi-structured interviews plus publicly available documents. It reports no regression and contains no tables and no figures, which is why the regression digest for this paper is empty.
Interviews lasted between 30 and 75 minutes, were conducted in the interviewees' native language and fully transcribed (PDF p. 7).

Thematic analysis in phases: each national team developed interpretative categories from its own material using first-order, informant-centric codes; categories were then compared and contrasted; the discussions produced a common coding template built on three thematic areas - labour market fluidity, role of passion and portfolio, labour market position - used as the common interpretative framework for all three cases (PDF p. 7).
Findings from the first analysis step were condensed in three national reports (Been et al., 2018; Bellini et al., 2018; Larsen et al., 2018).

Sector statistics are quoted from industry sources, not registers: European games market employment 86,953 in 2019 vs 77,916 the previous year (EGDF and ISFE, 2021); workforce around 3,850 in the Netherlands (Games Monitor, 2018), around 1,600 in Italy (IIDEA, 2021) and 850 full-time equivalents in Denmark (Producentforeningen, 2021); Danish turnover increase of 335% between 2009 and 2019 (Producentforeningen, 2017, 2021); average Danish company lifespan 5 years; freelancers 40% of developers in Italy and 51% in Denmark; 35% of Dutch companies are one-person companies, while 70% of jobs are in companies larger than 10 employees (Koops, 2016).
The article warns that 'difficulties in demarcating the industry' mean statistical information on the sector should be used carefully (PDF p. 9).

Page convention for this extraction: every `page` recorded in a quote or evidence record is a PDF page index of paper.pdf (1-23). The journal pagination is 1266-1288, so PDF page n corresponds to journal page 1265+n (PDF p. 10 = journal p. 1275).
